lessons.md:
A recruiter spends seconds on your CV. One page with numbers and links gets you to the interview; the interview gets you the job.

### The essentials

Recruiters spend seconds on a CV. Give them:

- A two-line summary: the role you want and your strongest proof.
- **Projects first** if you're switching careers: three lines each, with numbers ("hit rate at 5 from 0.71 to 0.86", "p95 2.4 s", "£0.003 per answer") and live links.
- Experience: rewrite past jobs as outcomes with numbers, and highlight anything with data, automation or stakeholders.
- Skills: only what you can discuss for ten minutes.

One page. No photo, no skill bars, no buzzword lists.

### Worked example

Turning a vague bullet into a strong one:

- Before: "Worked on a chatbot using Python and AI."
- After: "Built a RAG assistant over 60 NHS policies (FastAPI, pgvector); raised retrieval hit rate from 70% to 87% with hybrid search; live demo and code linked."

What you built, how, the result in a number, and where to see it.

### Common mistakes

- Listing every tool you've touched.
- No links to live projects.

### Try it

Rewrite your top three CV bullets in the after style.

lessons.md:
Your portfolio is the evidence behind your CV. Each project should be understandable in under a minute.

### The essentials

A GitHub profile README or a one-page site that links:

- The three projects: one line on the problem, a live demo, a two-minute video, the repo.
- A short case study for each: the user, the decisions, the numbers, what you'd do next.
- AI-103 badge and contact details.

Pin the three repos. Make sure every README has a screenshot in the first screen and every demo works on a phone.

### Worked example

A project case study opens with the problem and the result, then how:

> **Problem:** new staff couldn't find answers in 60 policies.
> **Result:** cited answers in about 2 seconds; 87% of test questions retrieved the right source.
> **How:** hybrid search, reranking, grounded prompts with refusal.
> **Links:** live demo, code, two-minute video.

Your project pages on benchwrk can be shared as exactly this.

### Common mistakes

- Starting with the tech stack.
- Dead demo links.

### Try it

Write the case study for project 1 and share its page.

lessons.md:
Applying widely but blindly wastes evenings. A target list keeps you focused on roles you can actually get.

### The essentials

List 40 employers across three bands:
- **AI-adjacent** roles (AI-enabled data, automation, analytics engineering) where you're competitive now.
- **Applied AI** teams in sectors you know (education, public sector, health, retail).
- **Stretch** roles at AI-first companies.

For each: why you, a contact (alumni, meetups, LinkedIn), the job page. Referrals convert far better than cold applications, so spend time on people as well as forms.

### Worked example

A tracker with columns: company, role, link, job title type (AI engineer, ML engineer, data or analytics with AI, solutions or support engineer), match out of 5, date applied, outcome. Include AI-adjacent roles where your current experience counts; they're often the quickest way in.

### Common mistakes

- Only applying to "AI Engineer" titles at big tech companies.
- Not tracking outcomes, so you can't see what's working.

### Try it

Find 20 live roles and score them. Apply to the top five this week.

o: You're competitive sooner and can move internally later

lessons.md:
Coding screens test whether you can think out loud and write working code under mild pressure. Practice makes them routine.

### The essentials

Most screens are easy to medium Python: strings, dicts, sorting, two pointers, simple recursion. Practise 30 problems, timed at 25 minutes each:

1. Restate the problem and ask one clarifying question.
2. Give the brute-force idea, then improve.
3. Write clean code with clear names; talk while you type.
4. Test with an edge case before saying done.

The exercises in this course are warm-ups in exactly that shape.

### Worked example

A repeatable approach:

1. Restate the problem and ask one clarifying question.
2. Give two examples, including an edge case.
3. Say a simple approach and its cost before coding.
4. Code it, talking as you go.
5. Test with your examples and fix calmly.

Most screens for these roles are practical (strings, dicts, parsing, small classes), not hard algorithms.

### Common mistakes

- Coding in silence.
- Jumping straight into code before agreeing the examples.

### Try it

Do the four practice exercises here, timing yourself and narrating out loud.

lessons.md:
Take-home tasks show how you'd work on the job. Reviewers care about clear choices more than extra features.

### The essentials

Do two mocks in six hours each: a small RAG app and an eval harness. What graders look for:

- A working core over many half-features.
- Tests on the logic that matters.
- A README with decisions, trade-offs and what you'd do with more time.
- Honest limits.

Time-box hard. Submitting on time with a clear "next steps" section beats an extra feature.

### Worked example

With a four-hour budget: 30 minutes planning and asking questions, two and a half hours building the core with tests, 30 minutes on the README (decisions, trade-offs, what you'd do next) and 30 minutes of slack. With one hour left, stop adding features and write up.

### Common mistakes

- Running over the time limit by a day.
- No README explaining your choices.

### Try it

Do a past take-home from a public repository in four hours, then review it against this plan.

check.q: With one hour left on a take-home, you should:
o: Tidy, test and write the README

lessons.md:
System design for AI apps checks whether you can turn a vague request into a sensible, safe, measurable system.

### The essentials

Practise two prompts out loud, recorded:
1. "Design a document Q&A assistant for 5,000 staff."
2. "Design a support agent that can look up orders and issue refunds."

A structure that works: requirements and numbers (users, documents, latency, budget), data flow (ingest, retrieve, generate), evaluation, safety and approvals, cost, monitoring, and what you'd build first. Use the tutor's mock interview below to rehearse follow-up questions.

### Worked example

A structure for any design question:

1. Users and the job to be done.
2. Requirements: speed, cost, accuracy, privacy.
3. Data: where it comes from and how it's updated.
4. The pipeline: retrieval, model, tools.
5. Evaluation and monitoring.
6. Risks and how you'd reduce them.

Draw boxes and arrows as you talk, and give numbers where you can.

### Common mistakes

- Starting with a vector database before asking who the users are.
- Forgetting evaluation and cost.

### Try it

Design a policy assistant for a 5,000-person company out loud in 20 minutes, recording yourself.

lessons.md:
Behavioural questions decide many offers. Stories from your current job count, especially if they show judgement and results.

### The essentials

Write six STAR stories (Situation, Task, Action, Result): conflict, failure, ownership, influence, ambiguity and delivery. Each takes about two minutes to tell.

- Keep the situation to two sentences; spend most time on **your** actions.
- End with a number or a concrete change, then one line on what you learned.
- Career switchers: past jobs are full of good stories. Use them.

Practise with the tutor's mock interview: it asks a question, you answer, it gives feedback.

### Worked example

A STAR story with most of the time on the action:

> **Situation:** monthly reports took two days by hand.
> **Task:** I was asked to speed them up.
> **Action:** I mapped the steps, automated the data pulls in Python, added checks for missing values and trained two colleagues.
> **Result:** reports took two hours; errors found before release went from three a month to none.

### Common mistakes

- Talking about "we" so much that your part is invisible.
- Stories with no result.

### Try it

Write five stories from your current job: a hard problem, a mistake, a disagreement, leading without authority and a result you're proud of.

lessons.md:
Job searches are a numbers game with feedback. A weekly routine keeps you moving and shows what to change.

### The essentials

Send 5 to 8 targeted applications a week. For each, tailor three CV lines to the advert, write a four-sentence note (why them, one proof, one link, a clear ask) and log it.

Track: date, company, role, route (referral or cold), stage and next step. Review on Sundays. If 20 applications produce no interviews, change the CV or the target list, not just the volume.

### Worked example

A weekly hour: apply to five tracked roles, follow up on last week's, ask one person in the field for a 15-minute chat and update your tracker. Every four weeks, look at the numbers: many applications and no interviews means fix the CV and targeting; interviews but no offers means practise interviews.

### Common mistakes

- Changing everything at once when results are slow.
- Stopping study entirely while applying.

### Try it

Book a recurring weekly hour for applications in your calendar.

o: The CV or the target list
